title: Hypertensive Heart Diseases: Systemic and Pulmonary Hypertension
subject: Cardiovascular System (CARD)

overview.intro: This chapter covers the damage that chronically raised pressure does in both circulations. In the systemic circuit, sustained hypertension thickens the left ventricle, narrows arterioles in the kidney, brain, and retina, and sets the stage for stroke, heart failure, kidney disease, and aortic dissection; a rapid, severe rise causes acute organ injury. In the pulmonary circuit, raised pressure remodels small pulmonary arteries and ends in right ventricular failure. Board questions reward mechanism: why low renin points to the adrenal, why a thick ventricle produces an S4, why onion-skin arterioles signal an emergency, and why a loud P2 with right axis deviation points to the lungs.
prerequisites: Determinants of arterial pressure: cardiac output, systemic vascular resistance, and pressure natriuresis
The renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system and adrenal cortex and medulla hormones
Ventricular wall stress (law of Laplace) and the atrial contribution to ventricular filling
Normal pulmonary circulation pressures and hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction
Endothelial mediators: nitric oxide, prostacyclin, and endothelin-1

connections.how: Concentric hypertrophy is a leading cause of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, and left heart failure is the most common cause of pulmonary hypertension.
Hypertension accelerates coronary atherosclerosis and makes a hypertrophied ventricle vulnerable to subendocardial ischemia.
Hypertension is a major risk factor for atherosclerosis and the most important risk factor for aortic dissection.
The kidney sets long-term pressure and is injured by it, and adrenal disorders produce secondary hypertension with predictable laboratory patterns.
Chronic lung disease, sleep apnea, and pulmonary embolism raise pulmonary vascular resistance and lead to cor pulmonale.

terms.def: Sustained high arterial pressure with no single identifiable cause, arising from many genetic and environmental influences.
Hypertension produced by a specific, identifiable disorder such as renal artery stenosis or primary aldosteronism.
The rise in renal sodium and water excretion that follows a rise in arterial pressure, which lets the kidney set long-term pressure.
Homogeneous pink, glassy thickening of arteriolar walls with a narrowed lumen, from leaked plasma proteins and excess matrix.
Concentric, laminated (onion-skin) thickening of arteriolar walls by smooth muscle cells and reduplicated basement membrane, typical of severe hypertension.
Necrosis of a vessel wall in which fibrin and other plasma proteins seep in, producing bright pink, smudgy material on routine stains.
Thickening of a ventricular wall with sarcomeres added in parallel, typical of pressure overload, with little chamber enlargement.
Impaired ventricular relaxation and filling, so a normal end-diastolic volume requires a higher filling pressure.
Severe blood pressure elevation, often 180/120 mmHg or higher, with new or worsening acute damage to target organs.
Mean pulmonary artery pressure above 20 mmHg at rest, measured by right heart catheterization.
Mean pulmonary artery pressure minus wedge pressure, divided by cardiac output, expressed in Wood units.
Right ventricular hypertrophy, dilation, or failure caused by pulmonary hypertension from disease of the lungs or pulmonary vessels, not from left heart disease.

sections.title: Defining systemic hypertension and the origins of primary hypertension

blocks.text: How blood pressure is classified

Cardiovascular risk rises continuously from a systolic pressure of about 115 mmHg, so any definition of hypertension is a chosen threshold. Under the 2017 American College of Cardiology and American Heart Association (ACC/AHA) guideline, which most United States board material follows, normal is below 120/80 mmHg, elevated is 120 to 129 systolic with diastolic below 80, stage 1 is 130 to 139 systolic or 80 to 89 diastolic, and stage 2 is 140 or higher systolic or 90 or higher diastolic. When the two values fall in different categories the higher one applies, so 128/86 mmHg is stage 1.

The diagnosis rests on the average of repeated readings on two or more occasions, ideally confirmed outside the office. White coat hypertension is high only in the office, from an alerting sympathetic response, and masked hypertension is high only outside it. Pressure normally falls about 10 to 20% during sleep, and loss of this dipping suggests sleep apnea, kidney disease, or autonomic dysfunction. Hypertension is usually silent until an organ is damaged, so it is found by measurement.
Why pressure stays high: the kidney

Mean arterial pressure equals cardiac output multiplied by systemic vascular resistance. In established primary hypertension, output is usually normal and resistance is raised. Baroreceptors defend pressure over minutes but reset within a day or two, so they cannot set long-term pressure. The kidney does: a rise in pressure increases sodium and water excretion (pressure natriuresis) until volume and pressure return to the level at which sodium output equals intake. Because this feedback has a very high gain, pressure can stay high only if the kidney's pressure to sodium excretion relationship shifts, so that a higher pressure is needed to excrete the daily salt load. Every chronic hypertension, primary or secondary, involves such a shift.
Primary hypertension is polygenic

Primary (essential) hypertension accounts for about 90 to 95% of cases. Inheritance explains roughly 30 to 50% of blood pressure variation, spread across hundreds of variants of small effect in renal sodium handling, the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS), vascular tone, and sympathetic control. Rare monogenic forms confirm the central role of renal salt handling. In Liddle syndrome, a gain-of-function mutation keeps the epithelial sodium channel (ENaC) of the collecting duct in the membrane, so sodium is reabsorbed regardless of aldosterone. In apparent mineralocorticoid excess, deficiency of 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 lets cortisol occupy the mineralocorticoid receptor, and glycyrrhetinic acid in licorice inhibits the same enzyme. Both inherited disorders produce early-onset hypertension with hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, and low renin and aldosterone.

blocks.title: Risk factors for primary hypertension
rows: Aortic stiffening raises systolic and pulse pressure and lowers diastolic pressure (isolated systolic hypertension)
Many small-effect variants; prevalence and severity are higher in Black adults in the United States
Hyperinsulinemia increases tubular sodium reabsorption, leptin raises sympathetic outflow, adipose tissue releases angiotensinogen; also promotes sleep apnea
Volume expansion in salt-sensitive people; low potassium favors distal sodium retention
Sympathetic and RAAS activation; pressure falls when intake stops
Higher sympathetic tone; contributes to obesity and insulin resistance
Nephron loss and arteriolar disease shift pressure natriuresis upward
blocks.caption: Each risk factor raises output, resistance, or renal sodium retention; most act through more than one.

sections.title: Secondary hypertension: identifiable causes and their clues

blocks.text: Secondary hypertension, about 5 to 10% of cases, has a specific cause. Suspect it when hypertension begins before about age 30 or abruptly, is severe or resistant, or comes with an unexpected finding such as hypokalemia. Chronic kidney disease of any cause is common, because fewer nephrons must excrete the same salt load.
Renal artery stenosis

A narrowed renal artery lowers afferent arteriolar pressure, so juxtaglomerular cells release renin as though the whole body were underperfused. Angiotensin II constricts arterioles and stimulates aldosterone, giving a high-renin, high-aldosterone state. Atherosclerosis causes most cases, in older adults with vascular disease, and narrows the ostium or proximal artery. Fibromuscular dysplasia, a noninflammatory and usually medial thickening, affects women about 15 to 50 years old, involves the mid to distal artery with a string of beads appearance, and can also involve the carotid and vertebral arteries. Clues include an abdominal bruit, hypokalemia, and a small kidney on the affected side. Filtration in the stenotic kidney depends on angiotensin II constricting the efferent arteriole, so blocking angiotensin II can sharply lower the glomerular filtration rate (GFR). Bilateral disease can cause recurrent flash pulmonary edema.
Adrenal causes

Primary aldosteronism, from bilateral adrenal hyperplasia or an aldosterone-producing adenoma (Conn syndrome), is the most common endocrine cause. Aldosterone opens more ENaC channels in principal cells, and the more negative lumen drives potassium secretion, while alpha-intercalated cells secrete more H+, producing metabolic alkalosis. Volume expansion suppresses renin, the key contrast with renal artery stenosis. Edema does not develop because rising pressure and atrial natriuretic peptide restore sodium balance within days (aldosterone escape), but potassium wasting continues, although many patients are normokalemic.

Pheochromocytoma, a catecholamine-secreting chromaffin cell tumor of the adrenal medulla (paraganglioma if extra-adrenal), raises resistance through alpha-1 receptors and output through beta-1 receptors. Episodic headache, sweating, and palpitations occur on sustained or fluctuating hypertension. Tumor catechol-O-methyltransferase forms metanephrines continuously, so plasma or urine metanephrines stay high between episodes. Epinephrine-secreting tumors are adrenal because cortisol from the cortex induces phenylethanolamine N-methyltransferase. Hereditary forms occur in MEN 2 (RET), von Hippel-Lindau disease, and neurofibromatosis type 1. In Cushing syndrome, cortisol overwhelms renal 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 and activates mineralocorticoid receptors, raises angiotensinogen, and increases vascular sensitivity to pressors.
Coarctation and sleep apnea

Adult coarctation narrows the aorta just distal to the left subclavian artery near the ligamentum arteriosum. The arms are hypertensive, femoral pulses are weak and delayed, and underperfused kidneys add renin. Intercostal collaterals notch the posterior ribs but spare ribs 1 and 2, whose posterior intercostal arteries arise from the costocervical trunk rather than the aorta. Coarctation is associated with a bicuspid aortic valve and Turner syndrome. In obstructive sleep apnea, each apnea causes hypoxemia and each arousal a sympathetic surge; repeated nightly, these raise daytime sympathetic tone and activate the RAAS, a common cause of resistant hypertension.

blocks.title: Secondary causes of hypertension
rows: Bruit, small kidney, GFR falls when angiotensin II is blocked
Cushingoid habitus, licorice intake, or early onset with hypokalemia
Episodic headache, sweating, palpitations; high metanephrines
Arm hypertension, weak delayed femoral pulses, rib notching
Snoring, daytime sleepiness, loss of nocturnal dipping
blocks.caption: Both high points to renal hypoperfusion, low renin with high aldosterone points to the adrenal cortex, and both low points to a mineralocorticoid effect from something other than aldosterone.

sections.title: Chronic hypertensive damage to arterioles, heart, kidney, retina, and brain

blocks.text: Hyaline arteriolosclerosis

Arterioles are the resistance vessels, so they bear the strain. Chronic stress lets plasma proteins leak through injured endothelium into the wall, and smooth muscle cells add basement membrane and matrix. The wall becomes homogeneous, pink, and glassy, and the narrowed lumen causes slow, patchy ischemia of the tissue supplied. The lesion is also typical of diabetes and appears mildly with aging.
The heart: concentric left ventricular hypertrophy

By the law of Laplace, wall stress is proportional to pressure times radius divided by twice the wall thickness. A higher afterload raises systolic wall stress, and myocytes respond by adding sarcomeres in parallel, becoming thicker with enlarged boxcar nuclei. The wall thickens with little chamber enlargement (concentric hypertrophy), which returns stress toward normal. Volume overload instead adds sarcomeres in series and dilates the chamber (eccentric hypertrophy). The normal left ventricular wall is about 1.0 to 1.5 cm and can approach or exceed 2 cm in hypertensive heart disease.

blocks.title: Pressure overload to diastolic failure and atrial fibrillation
steps: Sustained hypertension raises left ventricular afterload
Systolic wall stress rises (law of Laplace)
Sarcomeres added in parallel: concentric hypertrophy
Thick, fibrotic wall relaxes slowly and is stiff
Higher left atrial pressure is needed for filling
Left atrium dilates; pulmonary venous pressure rises
Atrial fibrillation and heart failure with preserved ejection fraction
blocks.caption: Concentric hypertrophy normalizes systolic wall stress at the price of a stiff ventricle; late in the course the ventricle can dilate and lose systolic function.

blocks.text: A stiff ventricle fills poorly in early diastole and depends on atrial contraction, so losing the atrial kick in atrial fibrillation can cause abrupt congestion. Greater muscle mass, lagging capillary density, and high diastolic pressure compressing subendocardial vessels make the hypertrophied wall prone to ischemia, worsened by accelerated coronary atherosclerosis. Atrial contraction into the stiff ventricle produces an S4. On the ECG, tall R waves in V5 and V6 with deep S waves in V1 reflect the larger mass, and lateral ST depression with T wave inversion forms the strain pattern.
Kidney, retina, and brain

In benign nephrosclerosis, hyaline afferent arterioles and thickened interlobular arteries cause glomerulosclerosis, tubular atrophy, and interstitial fibrosis, leaving symmetrically small kidneys with a finely granular surface, mild proteinuria, and slowly falling GFR. Hypertension is the second leading cause of end-stage kidney disease after diabetes, with higher risk in carriers of high-risk APOL1 variants. Lost nephrons impair sodium excretion and worsen the hypertension.

The retina shows arteriolar disease directly: narrowing, copper or silver wiring from a thickened wall, arteriovenous nicking where a thick arteriole compresses a vein in their shared sheath, flame hemorrhages, hard exudates, and cotton wool spots (nerve fiber layer microinfarcts).

Penetrating arteries such as the lenticulostriate branches of the middle cerebral artery receive nearly full parent pressure. Lipohyalinosis occludes them, causing lacunar infarcts under about 15 mm in the basal ganglia, internal capsule, thalamus, and pons. Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms weaken them, and rupture causes deep intracerebral hemorrhage, most often in the putamen, then thalamus, pons, and cerebellum, unlike the lobar hemorrhages of amyloid angiopathy. Hypertension is also the most important risk factor for aortic dissection.

blocks.predict: A 66-year-old man with long-standing hypertension develops atrial fibrillation and, within hours, becomes short of breath at rest although his ejection fraction is 60%. Why did losing atrial contraction affect him so severely?
blocks.explain: Concentric hypertrophy made his ventricle stiff and slow to relax, so it depends on atrial contraction for filling. Fibrillation removes that contribution and the fast rate shortens diastole, so filling falls and left atrial and pulmonary venous pressures rise despite preserved systolic function.

blocks.text: A hypertensive emergency is severe elevation, often 180/120 mmHg or higher, with new or worsening acute damage to a target organ. Equally high pressure without acute damage is sometimes called hypertensive urgency. The older term malignant hypertension (severe hypertension with retinal hemorrhages, exudates, or papilledema, often with acute kidney injury) is now considered a form of emergency. The rate of rise and the failure of protective mechanisms matter more than the level reached.
Autoregulation and breakthrough

The brain and kidney keep flow nearly constant across a range of pressures by arteriolar constriction and dilation, in the brain roughly 60 to 150 mmHg mean arterial pressure. Chronic hypertension shifts this curve to the right. Above the upper limit, constriction is forced open (breakthrough), capillaries meet full arterial pressure, and the blood-brain barrier leaks, causing vasogenic edema and hypertensive encephalopathy with headache, confusion, visual disturbance, and seizures. The edema often favors the posterior circulation, which has less sympathetic innervation (posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome). A previously normotensive person has an unshifted curve and breaks through at lower pressure, as in eclampsia or acute glomerulonephritis.
The acute arteriolar lesion

A rapid, severe rise injures arteriolar endothelium, plasma proteins and fibrin enter the wall, and smooth muscle cells die, producing fibrinoid necrosis (bright pink, smudgy wall, often with luminal thrombus). Surviving arterioles respond with concentric layers of smooth muscle and reduplicated basement membrane, the onion-skin lesion of hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis, most conspicuous in renal interlobular arteries and afferent arterioles. The same lesion occurs in scleroderma renal crisis and other thrombotic microangiopathies.

Hyaline: glassy wall from protein leak and matrix
Hyperplastic onion-skin layering with fibrinoid necrosis
Acute pulmonary edema, acute coronary syndrome
Lacunes, deep hemorrhage; arteriolar narrowing, AV nicking
Benign nephrosclerosis: small, finely granular kidneys

blocks.caption: Glassy thickening marks chronic moderate pressure; onion-skin layering with fibrinoid necrosis marks severe, accelerated pressure with acute organ injury.

blocks.title: The renal vicious cycle of hypertensive emergency
steps: Severe rise in arterial pressure
Fibrinoid necrosis and onion-skin narrowing of renal arterioles
Glomerular ischemia downstream
Juxtaglomerular cells release large amounts of renin
Angiotensin II constricts arterioles; pressure natriuresis shrinks volume and adds renin
Pressure rises further and injures more arterioles
blocks.caption: Arteriolar injury causes renal ischemia, ischemia drives renin release, and renin raises pressure, which injures more arterioles.

blocks.text: Other acute injuries follow the same logic. Sudden afterload can cause left ventricular failure or ischemia, shear stress can tear the aortic intima (dissection), and fibrin strands in damaged small vessels shear red cells into schistocytes, causing microangiopathic hemolytic anemia with thrombocytopenia and raised lactate dehydrogenase. Triggers include untreated primary hypertension, renovascular disease, glomerulonephritis, scleroderma renal crisis, preeclampsia, pheochromocytoma, cocaine or amphetamines, and abrupt clonidine withdrawal, which causes a rebound sympathetic surge.

blocks.predict: A 72-year-old woman with 30 years of hypertension has a pressure of 186/112 mmHg with no symptoms and a normal fundus. A previously normotensive 24-year-old woman at 36 weeks of pregnancy has 168/108 mmHg with headache and confusion. Which has a hypertensive emergency, and why did the lower pressure cause more harm?
blocks.explain: The pregnant woman. Her autoregulation curve has not shifted right, so 168/108 mmHg exceeds her upper limit, causing breakthrough, vasogenic edema, and encephalopathy. The older woman has severe hypertension without acute organ damage.
blocks.check: Compare with the subsection on autoregulation and breakthrough.

blocks.text: The pulmonary circulation carries the whole cardiac output at about 25/8 mmHg (mean about 14 mmHg), with a resistance about one tenth of systemic resistance or less. During exercise, recruitment and distension of capillaries lower resistance as flow rises. The thin-walled right ventricle handles volume well but tolerates a rise in pressure poorly.
Definition and hemodynamic types

Pulmonary hypertension is a mean pulmonary artery pressure above 20 mmHg at rest on right heart catheterization (the 2018 World Symposium threshold; many textbooks still quote 25 mmHg). Echocardiography estimates systolic pressure from the tricuspid regurgitant jet and raises suspicion. Mean pressure equals cardiac output times pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) plus left atrial pressure, estimated by the wedge pressure. Precapillary disease has a wedge pressure of 15 mmHg or less and a PVR above 2 Wood units. Isolated postcapillary disease has a wedge pressure above 15 mmHg and a PVR of 2 or less. Combined disease has both a high wedge pressure and a high PVR. One Wood unit equals 1 mmHg per L/min.

blocks.title: Separating precapillary from postcapillary pulmonary hypertension
blocks.text: Two patients each have a mean pulmonary artery pressure of 36 mmHg and a cardiac output of 5 L/min. Patient A has a wedge pressure of 10 mmHg; patient B, 28 mmHg. PVR is (mean pressure minus wedge pressure) divided by cardiac output. For A, (36 minus 10) / 5 = 5.2 Wood units with a normal wedge: the disease is in the pulmonary arteries or lung, as in pulmonary arterial hypertension, lung disease, or chronic thromboembolism. For B, (36 minus 28) / 5 = 1.6 Wood units, which is normal: high left atrial pressure is being transmitted backward, as in left ventricular failure or mitral stenosis. The same mean pressure reflects different diseases.
Classification by cause

blocks.title: Clinical classification of pulmonary hypertension
rows: Disease of small pulmonary arteries: endothelial dysfunction, constriction, proliferative remodeling
Idiopathic; heritable (BMPR2); anorexigens, methamphetamine; systemic sclerosis; HIV; portal hypertension; congenital shunts; schistosomiasis
High left atrial pressure transmitted backward
Heart failure with reduced or preserved ejection fraction, mitral and aortic valve disease
COPD, interstitial lung disease, sleep apnea, hypoventilation, high altitude
Organized thrombi obstruct arteries; open vessels remodel
blocks.caption: Group 2 is the most common cause, followed by group 3; group 1 is uncommon but the most tested for molecular pathogenesis.

blocks.text: In group 2, high left atrial pressure first raises pulmonary pressure passively, but persistent venous hypertension, classically from long-standing mitral stenosis, can remodel the arteries and add a precapillary component. In group 3, low alveolar oxygen closes oxygen-sensitive K+ channels in pulmonary arterial smooth muscle, the cells depolarize, L-type Ca2+ channels open, and the muscle contracts. This diverts blood from poorly ventilated alveoli locally, but global hypoxia constricts the whole lung and drives medial hypertrophy, while hypoxemia-driven polycythemia raises viscosity. In group 4, a small minority of pulmonary emboli organize into fibrous webs instead of lysing; ventilation-perfusion scanning shows mismatched perfusion defects.

sections.title: Pathogenesis of pulmonary arterial hypertension and its effects on the right heart

blocks.text: Genetic and acquired triggers

Heritable pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is most often caused by loss-of-function mutations in BMPR2, a receptor of the transforming growth factor beta superfamily whose SMAD signaling restrains smooth muscle proliferation and promotes apoptosis. Inheritance is autosomal dominant with incomplete penetrance, so a second hit such as inflammation or hypoxia is thought to be needed. Idiopathic PAH is more common in women. Acquired triggers include serotonergic anorexigens such as fenfluramine (serotonin is a smooth muscle mitogen), systemic sclerosis, HIV, and portal hypertension. A large left-to-right shunt remodels the arteries until resistance exceeds systemic resistance and the shunt reverses (Eisenmenger syndrome). In hepatosplenic Schistosoma mansoni infection, eggs reach the lungs through portosystemic collaterals and provoke granulomatous arteriolar injury.

blocks.title: Endothelial mediators in pulmonary arterial hypertension
rows: Soluble guanylyl cyclase, cGMP: dilation, antiproliferative
IP receptor, Gs, cAMP: dilation, inhibits platelets
ETA receptor, Gq, Ca2+: constriction, mitogen
blocks.caption: Too little of two dilator and antiproliferative signals and too much of one constrictor and mitogen.

blocks.title: Pathogenesis of pulmonary arterial hypertension
steps: BMPR2 loss or another trigger injures endothelium
Nitric oxide and prostacyclin fall; endothelin-1 and thromboxane rise
Small arteries constrict; in situ thrombi form
Apoptosis-resistant smooth muscle proliferates
Medial hypertrophy, intimal fibrosis, plexiform lesions
Pulmonary vascular resistance becomes fixed
Right ventricular hypertrophy, then failure (cor pulmonale)
blocks.caption: Endothelial imbalance starts the process, proliferative remodeling makes it permanent, and the right ventricle bears the load.

blocks.text: Medial hypertrophy and muscularization of normally nonmuscular arterioles come first, then concentric intimal fibrosis. In severe idiopathic, heritable, and shunt-related disease, plexiform lesions form: tufts of slit-like endothelial channels at small artery branch points that resemble a glomerulus. Large pulmonary arteries develop atherosclerotic plaques, which normally do not form at pulmonary pressures.
The right ventricle and cor pulmonale

The right ventricle first hypertrophies concentrically, then dilates. Dilation stretches the tricuspid annulus (regurgitation) and pushes the septum left into a D shape, limiting left ventricular filling. When right ventricular pressure nears systemic, its normal systolic coronary perfusion is lost while demand rises, so ischemia accelerates failure. Cor pulmonale is right ventricular hypertrophy, dilation, or failure from disease of the lungs or pulmonary vessels, excluding left heart and congenital heart disease; it is chronic and hypertrophic in COPD or PAH, and acute and dilated after massive pulmonary embolism. Exertional dyspnea and fatigue come first; exertional syncope means output cannot rise across a fixed resistance. A dilated pulmonary artery can compress the left recurrent laryngeal nerve, causing hoarseness.

blocks.title: Findings in pulmonary hypertension and their mechanisms
rows: High pulmonary artery diastolic pressure closes the pulmonic valve forcefully
Holosystolic murmur louder on inspiration; large v waves
Right axis deviation, tall R in V1, P pulmonale
Right ventricular mass and right atrial enlargement
blocks.caption: Each sign reflects the pressure-loaded right heart or the high-pressure pulmonary artery.

blocks.predict: Why can a patient with severe pulmonary arterial hypertension have low systemic pressure even though the left heart is structurally normal?
blocks.explain: The right ventricle cannot push enough blood across the high resistance, so left atrial return falls, and the dilated right ventricle shifts the septum left and restricts left ventricular filling. Low preload lowers stroke volume and systemic pressure.
blocks.check: Compare with the subsection on the right ventricle and cor pulmonale.

integration.text: Anatomy and biochemistry explain where and why. Coarctation forms near the ligamentum arteriosum, so the arms are hypertensive and rib notching spares ribs 1 and 2, which are not supplied from the aorta; lenticulostriate arteries leave the middle cerebral artery at right angles, so hypertensive bleeds and lacunes cluster deep. The adrenal is a lesson in enzymes: 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 shields the mineralocorticoid receptor from cortisol, cortisol induces the enzyme that makes epinephrine, and catechol-O-methyltransferase produces the metanephrines that reveal pheochromocytoma. Systemic and pulmonary arterioles respond oppositely to hypoxia, which is why lung disease raises only pulmonary resistance.

Pathology ties the chapter together through three responses: hyaline thickening under chronic moderate pressure, onion-skin proliferation with fibrinoid necrosis under acute severe pressure, and concentric hypertrophy of whichever ventricle faces the load. These patterns have limits. Hyaline change also occurs with diabetes and aging, onion-skin arterioles also occur in scleroderma renal crisis, and one patient often has several mechanisms at once, such as obesity, sleep apnea, and primary aldosteronism together.

summary: Under the 2017 ACC/AHA scheme, stage 1 hypertension is 130 to 139 systolic or 80 to 89 diastolic mmHg and stage 2 is 140/90 mmHg or higher, based on repeated readings.
Primary hypertension (about 90 to 95%) is polygenic, and because the kidney sets long-term pressure, every sustained hypertension involves a shift in pressure natriuresis.

Renal artery stenosis raises renin and aldosterone; primary aldosteronism raises aldosterone with low renin, hypokalemia, and alkalosis but no edema; low renin with low aldosterone suggests Cushing syndrome, licorice, or Liddle syndrome.
Pheochromocytoma causes episodic headache, sweating, and palpitations with high metanephrines; coarctation causes arm hypertension, weak delayed femoral pulses, and rib notching.

Chronic hypertension causes hyaline arteriolosclerosis, benign nephrosclerosis, retinal arteriolar changes, lacunes, and deep hemorrhage from Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms, most often in the putamen.
Pressure overload causes concentric left ventricular hypertrophy that normalizes wall stress but produces diastolic dysfunction, an S4, left atrial enlargement, and atrial fibrillation.

Hypertensive emergency is severe elevation with acute organ damage; its lesion is onion-skin hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis with fibrinoid necrosis, and renal ischemia drives a high-renin vicious cycle.

Pulmonary hypertension is a mean pulmonary artery pressure above 20 mmHg; precapillary disease has a normal wedge pressure and a PVR above 2 Wood units, and left heart disease (group 2) is the most common cause.
Pulmonary arterial hypertension combines BMPR2-related loss of a growth brake with low nitric oxide and prostacyclin and high endothelin-1, producing remodeling and plexiform lesions.
Right ventricular pressure overload explains a loud P2, a parasternal heave, right axis deviation, and, with failure, tricuspid regurgitation, raised venous pressure, and edema (cor pulmonale).

verify: Blood pressure categories follow the 2017 ACC/AHA guideline (stage 1 from 130/80 mmHg). The 2025 AHA/ACC update is understood to keep these categories, while European guidelines still define hypertension from 140/90 mmHg; confirm which scheme NABNE uses.

Pulmonary hypertension is defined here as mean pulmonary artery pressure above 20 mmHg (2018 World Symposium) with precapillary resistance above 2 Wood units (2022 ESC/ERS guideline; the 2018 World Symposium used 3 Wood units or more). Many textbooks still give 25 mmHg and 3 Wood units; confirm the values NABNE expects. The group classification was revised again at the 7th World Symposium in 2024 without changing the five main groups.
Prevalence of primary aldosteronism and the relative frequency of bilateral hyperplasia versus adenoma differ between studies and screening methods.
The share of hypertension that is secondary (about 5 to 10%) and the heritability of blood pressure (about 30 to 50%) are consensus approximations that vary by source.
Normal left ventricular wall thickness (about 1.0 to 1.5 cm) and hypertrophied thickness (near or above 2 cm) are approximate and vary with body size and source.
The cerebral autoregulatory range is quoted from about 50 to 150 mmHg or 60 to 160 mmHg in different references; this chapter uses roughly 60 to 150 mmHg.

The contribution of Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms to hypertensive intracerebral hemorrhage is debated in neuropathology, with some authors emphasizing lipohyalinosis; the competency and standard pathology texts present the microaneurysm explanation.
Confirm whether NABNE expects the eponyms Conn syndrome, Eisenmenger syndrome, and Charcot-Bouchard.

Drug and toxin associations with pulmonary arterial hypertension are periodically reclassified (definite versus possible); fenfluramine-related anorexigens and methamphetamine are listed here as established associations.

Requested new diagram names for a future revision: lvh-concentric-eccentric (normal, concentric, and eccentric ventricles in cross section) and arteriolosclerosis-types (hyaline versus hyperplastic onion-skin arteriole).
